stories.title_en: Blinding and Maiming: The Swindle of Crippling Victims

paragraphs.en: In Zhejiang there is a gang of swindlers who haunt busy thoroughfares and lonely byways, waiting for children of ten years or so belonging to others. Any child who loses their way home is sure to be carried off. They pick out girls who are pretty and quick-witted and sell them into brothels as prostitutes. The duller ones they blind in both eyes and teach to sing begging songs along the road; or they sever their feet at the ankle to leave the child lame. Their method of amputation is this: in deepest winter, when the cold is most bitter, they bind a child’s calves with hemp and set the feet in cold water. After a long soak they prod them with a stick of firewood and ask, “Does it hurt?” If the child answers, “It hurts,” they soak them longer, until the cold has congealed the blood and the prodding no longer hurts; then they slice off the foot with a sharp blade and dress the wound with medicine. Afterward they drive these blind and crippled children onto the roads to beg, demanding a daily take of money and rice. Those who bring back plenty get a full meal; those who bring back little are savagely beaten, so the young beggars learn to plead piteously. At night they all gather to sleep in a boat. The swindlers pocket the money and rice, dress in fine clothes, eat well, and amuse themselves singing on board. In idle hours they go ashore and fan out to kidnap more children. They are a monstrous plague on the people, and no one knows it.

One day, a female beggar was singing for alms on the road. An old woman living nearby said, "This beggar looks just like Li Yiwu's daughter—and her voice is like hers too, only she is blind." The beggar replied, "My father is indeed Li Yiwu; I have a brother named Ya'er. Five years ago, while going to my grandmother's house, I didn't know the way and was led away by someone who stabbed out both my eyes. Since then, he sends me out begging daily. If I bring back money and rice, I get food; if I collect little, I am beaten and starved—my suffering is unbearable. Your voice sounds exactly like my neighbor Auntie Wang Er. Please call my mother and brother to identify me and rescue me from this hell; your hidden merit will be as vast as Heaven." Auntie Wang Er heard her story and found every detail true. She took her home and said, "Your mother died this year, and your brother has moved to Upper Lane; I will send for him at once." They recognized each other immediately and filed a complaint with the county magistrate, who assigned it to the registrar for trial. Officials brought the two swindlers from their boat. The swindlers immediately bribed the registrar with silver, and paid another twenty taels to buy off the brother, Li Ya'er, saying, "Your sister was kidnapped by someone else; I merely took her in to join my band of beggars—it was not I who blinded her. Besides, she is now blind in both eyes and no one will marry her. It is better she stay with the beggars as a companion; she will not lack food or clothing." Having taken the silver, both the brother and the registrar failed to uphold the truth during the hearing, and the registrar ruled to return the girl to the swindlers. They took her to the boat, rowed out into the middle of the lake, and beat her savagely as a warning to other beggars never to let the secret out. Beggar Li cried her innocence to high heaven; the anguish was unbearable to hear.

The boat happened to come by the back gate of a retired official named Xiang. Hearing cries of mortal agony from the creek—pitiful beyond words—he sent two servants to haul the boat in and asked who was being beaten. The beggars pointed and said, “They are beating the beggar woman Li.” The official asked why. The woman dared not say; she only begged in her misery to be saved. He had her led apart from the others and asked again: “Why were you beaten so cruelly? Tell me plainly, and I will save you.” The beggar woman Li told the whole story from the beginning. Hearing it, Xiang was grief-stricken and could not contain his fury. He clapped the four crooks in chains on the spot, led the whole band of beggars in to see the prefect, and laid out their wrongs on their behalf. The prefect too burned with hatred. He had each of the four given thirty strokes and declared: “For a crime like this, even death by slow slicing would not be punishment enough. Chain them in front of the prefecture gate and let the crowd beat them, to vent the people’s rage.” Everyone who knew what these crooks had done came to strike them with fists and stones; in moments the four were torn and vomiting blood, and all died on the spot. Afterward, the blind and crippled beggars were each asked their native place. Those with families were sent home to be cared for; those without kin were placed in poorhouses. The people were all grateful for Xiang’s humanity in rooting out these four swindling fiends.

Note: People with young children must never let them go about alone, nor let them wear gold or silver bangles. Should a child chance to meet such crooks, regret comes too late. Guard against the loss before it happens. Henceforth, whenever officials come upon a place where blind and crippled beggars gather, they should send men to find out where they lodge and question one or two of them about how they came to be lame or blind. If crooks like these are unearthed, then removing one crook is better than removing a wolf or a tiger—and the merit of it is higher than any pagoda.

stories.title_en: A Eunuch Cooks Men and Eats Their Essence

paragraphs.en: The court time and again heeds ministers who preach profit and sends eunuchs out across the country to levy duties on goods—in the name of “taxing merchants and curbing the secondary trades to strengthen agriculture, the root.” In truth, when taxes on trade are heavy, goods grow dear wherever they are resold: prices rise for the buyer, and the buyer suffers. When trade stops moving, goods grow cheap where they are produced: prices fall for the seller, and the seller suffers. The profit may seem to come only from merchants, but all four classes of the people are silently bled of their wealth to feed the court’s hidden exactions—worse than openly raising the land tax. Worse still, of every levy taken, the court gets one share, the eunuch ten, the tax officials a hundred, and the patrol guards a thousand. So the people pay out hundreds or thousands of taels to deliver a single tael to the court: little gained above, measureless harm below. And yet, when runners and tax clerks stuff their bottomless gullets, at least it is folk of this same realm who get fed and warmed. But men who neither plow nor weave and yet make fish and meat of the common people are nothing but grubs, battening on the food and clothing of the world. As for the eunuchs: having plundered and squeezed until their hoards pile high and overflow, they look on brocade as dead leaves and on gold and jade as rubble. Their dress, their food, their vessels all match the Son of Heaven’s, and the minions at their beck and call wait on them as they would wait on the Son of Heaven. Of every blessing and pleasure the human world holds, they enjoy the uttermost; their one regret is that they cannot have the pleasure of women—that alone is denied them. One of them once bade his attendants hunt for a method to regrow the male organ, with ten thousand taels as the reward.

A wandering Daoist, greedy for that gold, made a wild guess of his own: “The old formulas say earth is mended with earth, wood is mended with wood, man is mended with man—so eating human flesh must mend a man.” He went recklessly and offered up a recipe: “Boil a young boy, mince the liver, dry the flesh, and eat the essence and marrow. Then the vital fluid will be replenished, the organ will grow back, and you can lie with women and father sons.” The eunuch Gao of Fujian believed him. He paid a hundred taels up front; if the dose proved effective, the man could return for ten thousand taels. From then on he sent his henchmen into poor villages and remote counties to buy young boys from destitute families, lying that “the Gao household wants to raise them as sons, and later they will have wealth and honor without end.” The poor believed it, and many sold their sons for the heavy profit in hand, hoping besides for riches to come. How many were bought in all is impossible to reckon. But some of the families who had sold sons sent people to ask after their boys—and there was never any word. Even the servants who ran errands in the yamen had no idea how the adopted sons inside were faring. In fact, the purchased boys were all kept in brocade and fed the finest food. Any cook who could prepare a boy for the table was rewarded with ten taels, and the secret was guarded under the strictest ban. Each time a boy was to be killed, the cook chased the children with a knife while they ran weeping and screaming; when they had run themselves hot and their blood was up, he seized a fat one and cooked him.

Among the boys was one of twelve who knelt before the cook, weeping and pleading, knocking his head on the ground and begging for his life. The cook wept too: “How could I save you? I fell into this against my own will as well.” Presently word came from outside that a certain retired official had come to pay a call. The cook said: “I will leave it to your fate: I am letting you out. A retired official is calling—grab his sleeve and wail for your life. If he will take you away, you may live, and I will die in your place. And tell the people outside: never sell a son into a eunuch’s house.” The boy ran straight to the official and cried out, “The cook is going to kill me!” The eunuch at once ordered the cook seized and beheaded—he hated him for letting the boy slip out—and with a smiling face commanded the boy to return inside. The boy clung desperately to the official’s sleeve, begging to be saved. The official suspected there was more behind it and took the boy out with him. The boy recounted in full how the children inside were being slaughtered, and the official sighed without end. But reflecting that he had never learned how the boys had been bought in the first place, and that with the cook dead there was no witness, he dared not keep the boy himself; he sent him out to find some other way to live. The boy later drifted as a beggar around Jian Prefecture and thereabouts. When people asked him about the eunuch’s household, he could tell them much of the wealth and splendor within—things this world has never seen. Only then did people learn that the eunuch ate human flesh, and only then did they refuse to sell their sons. In recent years Eunuch Gao was removed for his crimes. The parents who had sold their sons waited along the road in scores and hundreds, and not one saw a young son come out alive with that vile eunuch. There was none who did not shed tears, grieving that his boy must surely have been cooked.

Note: For poor people to sell their sons is folly of the deepest kind. If you cannot raise them, why not do as they do in Fengyang Prefecture, where father and son beg together? At least flesh and blood stay together. If there is truly no other way, sell them only to a rich household as servants. You must never feed them to a eunuch’s appetite, nor sell them into convents and temples as boy servants and attendants—that degradation is lower than beggary itself. The state keeps eunuchs to sweep the palace and carry messages, nothing more. To let them grasp the power of profit, glut themselves on every luxury, and then attempt to restore their virility so they can debauch women—a thing they cannot possibly have! Even if eating human flesh could feed your lust and prop up your rotting carcass, have you no pity for another person’s whole and unbroken life? If this can be endured, what cannot be endured? Mencius said, “Those skilled in war should suffer the heaviest punishment”—and that was for killing to make an army strong. What cause is this, that human lives should be treated as weeds? If the law of the land were truly enforced, this eunuch would never have been allowed to return alive.
